The SystemVerilog can be generated with:\n12\t\n13\t``` bash\n14\tbazel build //hdl/chisel/src/coralnpu:core_mini_axi_cc_library_emit_verilog\n15\t```\n16\t\n17\t### Module interfaces\n18\t\n19\t![CoralNPU AXI](images/coralnpu_axi.svg)\n20\t\n21\tThe interfaces to CoralNPU are defined as follows:\n22\t\n23\t|   Signal Bundle  |                   Description                             |\n24\t| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |\n25\t|       clk        | The clock of the AXI Bus/CoralNPU core.                     |\n26\t|      reset       | The active-low reset signal for the AXI Bus/CoralNPU core.  |\n27\t|      s_axi       | An AXI4 slave interface that can be used to write TCMs or touch CoralNPU CSRs. |\n28\t|      m_axi       | An AXI4 master interface used by CoralNPU to read/write to memories/CSRs. |\n29\t|       irqn       | Active-low interrupt to the CoralNPU core. Can be triggered by peripherals or other host processor. |\n30\t|       wfi        | Active-high signal from the CoralNPU core, indicating that the core is waiting for an interrupt. While this is active, CoralNPU is clock-gated. |\n31\t|      debug       | Debug interface to monitor CoralNPU instructions execution. This interface is typically only used for simulation. |\n32\t|      halted      | Output interface informing if the Core is running or not. Can be ignored. |\n33\t|      fault       | Output interface to determine if the Core hit a fault. These signals should be connected to a system control CPU interrupt-line or status register for notification when CoralNPU faults or is halted. |\n34\t\n35\t#### AXI master signals\n36\t\n37\tAR / AW channel\n38\t\n39\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n40\t| ------ | --------- |\n41\t| addr   | Address CoralNPU wishes to read/write |\n42\t| prot   | Always 2 (unprivileged, insecure, data) |\n43\t| id     | Always 0 |\n44\t| len    | (Count of beats in the burst) - 1 |\n45\t| size   | Bytes-per-beat (1, 2, or 4) |\n46\t| burst  | Always 1 (INCR) |\n47\t| lock   | Always 0 (normal access) |\n48\t| cache  | Always 0 (Device non-bufferable) |\n49\t| qos    | Always 0 |\n50\t| region | Always 0 |\n51\t\n52\tR channel\n53\t\n54\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n55\t| ------ | --------- |\n56\t| data   | Response data from the slave |\n57\t| id     | Ignored, but should be 0 as CoralNPU only emits txns with an id of 0 |\n58\t| resp   | Response code |\n59\t| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |\n60\t\n61\tW channel\n62\t\n63\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n64\t| ------ | --------- |\n65\t| data   | Data CoralNPU wishes to write |\n66\t| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |\n67\t| strb   | Which bytes in the data are valid |\n68\t\n69\tB channel\n70\t\n71\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n72\t| ------ | --------- |\n73\t| id     | Ignored, but should be 0 as CoralNPU only emits txns with an id of 0 (an RTL assertion exists for this) |\n74\t| resp   | Response code |\n75\t\n76\tNote: the USER signal is not supported on any of the channels.\n77\t\n78\t#### AXI slave signals\n79\t\n80\tAR / AW channel\n81\t\n82\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n83\t| ------ | --------- |\n84\t| addr   | Address the master wishes to read / write to |\n85\t| prot   | Ignored |\n86\t| id     | Transaction ID, should be reflected in the response beats |\n87\t| len    | (Count of beats in the burst) - 1 |\n88\t| size   | Bytes-per-beat (1,2,4,8,16) |\n89\t| burst  | 0, 1, or 2 (FIXED, INCR, WRAP) |\n90\t| lock   | Ignored |\n91\t| cache  | Ignored |\n92\t| qos    | Ignored |\n93\t| region | Ignored |\n94\t\n95\tR channel\n96\t\n97\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n98\t| ------ | --------- |\n99\t| data   | Response data from CoralNPU |\n100\t| id     | Transaction ID, should match with the id field from AR |\n101\t| resp   | Response code (0/OKAY or 2/SLVERR) |\n102\t| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |\n103\t\n104\tW channel\n105\t\n106\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n107\t| ------ | --------- |\n108\t| data   | Data the master wishes to write to CoralNPU |\n109\t| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |\n110\t| strb   | Which bytes in data are valid |\n111\t\n112\tB channel\n113\t\n114\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n115\t| ------ | --------- |\n116\t| id     | reset strategy -- to ensure proper reset behavior, ensure that the clock runs for a cycle with reset active, before enabling either the internal clock gate (via CSR) or gating externally.\n168\t\n169\t## Booting CoralNPU\n170\tA note first -- in these examples, CoralNPU is located in the overall system memory map at 0x70000000.\n171\t\n172\t1. The instruction memory of CoralNPU must be initialized.\n173\t```c\n174\tvolatile uint8_t* coralnpu_itcm = (uint8_t*)0x00000000L;\n175\tfor (int i = 0; i < coralnpu_binary_len; ++i) {\n176\t    coralnpu_itcm[i] = coralnpu_binary[i];\n177\t}\n178\t```\n179\t\n180\tIf something like a DMA engine is present in your system, that is probably a better option for initializing the ITCM.\n181\t\n182\t2. Program the start PC\n183\tIf your program is linked such that the starting address is 0, you may skip this.\n184\t\n185\t```c\n186\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_pc_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030004L;\n187\t*coralnpu_pc_csr = start_addr;\n188\t```\n189\t\n190\t3. Release clock gate\n191\t```c\n192\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_reset_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030000L;\n193\t*coralnpu_reset_csr = 1;\n194\t```\n195\t\n196\tAfter this, ensure you wait a cycle to allow CoralNPU's reset to occur.\n197\tIf you want to configure something like an interrupt that is connected to CoralNPU's\n198\tfault or halted outputs, this is a good time.\n199\t\n200\t4. Release reset\n201\t```c\n202\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_reset_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030000L;\n203\t*coralnpu_reset_csr = 0;\n204\t```\n205\t\n206\tAt this point, CoralNPU will begin executing at the PC programmed in step 2.\n207\t\n208\t5. Monitor for `io_halted`\n209\tThe status of CoralNPU's execution can be checked by reading the status CSR:\n210\t```c\n211\tvolatile uint32_t* coralnpu_status_csr = (uint32_t*)0x00030008L;\n212\tuint32_t status = *coralnpu_status_csr;\n213\tbool halted = status & 1;\n214\tbool fault = status & 2;\n215\t```\n216\t\n217\t# CoralNPU CSRs\n218\tNote: These are CSRs that are intended to be read or written externally\n219\tto CoralNPU, e.g. by the host processor in a system.\n220\tThey are not the same as the RISC-V CSRs accessed via the Zicsr ISA extension.\n221\t\n222\t### Register: `RESET_CONTROL`\n223\t*   **Offset**: `0x0`\n224\t*   **Description**: Controls reset and clock gating for the CoralNPU core. The design\n5\tof CoralNPU starts with domain and matrix capabilities; vector and scalar\n6\tcapabilities are then added for a fused design.\n7\t\n8\t## Block Diagram\n9\t\n10\t![CoralNPU block diagram](images/coralnpu_block.png)\n11\t\n12\t## Scalar Core\n13\t\n14\tA simple RISC-V scalar frontend drives the command queues of the ML+SIMD\n15\tbackend.\n16\t\n17\tCoralNPU utilizes a custom RISC-V frontend (rv32im) that runs the minimal set of\n18\tinstructions to support an executor run-to-completion model (eg. no OS, no\n19\tinterrupts), with all control tasks onloaded to the SMC . The C extension\n20\tencoding is reclaimed (as per the risc-v specification) to provide the necessary\n21\tencoding space for the SIMD registers (6b indices), and to allow flexible type\n22\tencodings and instruction compression (stripmining) for the SIMD instruction\n23\tset. The scalar core is an in order machine with no speculation.\n24\t\n25\tThe branch policy in the fetch stage is backwards branches are taken and forward\n26\tbranches are not-taken, incurring a penalty cycle if the execute result does not\n27\tmatch the decision in the fetch unit.\n28\t\n29\tRegisters        | Names         | Width\n30\t---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------\n31\tScalar (31)      | zero, x1..x31 | 32 bits\n32\tControl & Status | CSRx          | Various\n33\t\n34\t## Vector Core\n35\t\n36\tWe use SIMD and vector interchangeably, referring to a simple and practical SIMD\n37\tinstruction definition devoid of variable length behaviors. The scalar frontend\n38\tis decoupled from the backend by a FIFO structure that buffers vector\n39\tinstructions, posting only to the relevant command queues when dependencies are\n40\tresolved in the vector regfile. The vector core supports data widths of 8, 16, and 32 bits.\n41\t\n42\tRegisters        | Names         | Width\n43\t---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------\n44\tVector (64)      | v0..v63       | 256 bits (eg. int32 x8)\n45\tAccumulator      | acc<8><8>     | 8x8x 32 bits\n46\t\n47\t\n48\t### MAC\n49\t\n50\tThe central component of the design is a quantized outer product\n51\tmultiply-accumulate engine. An outer-product engine provides two-dimensional\n52\tbroadcast structures to maximize the amount of deliverable compute with respect\n53\tto memory accesses. On one axis is a parallel broadcast (“wide”, convolution\n54\tweights), and the other axis the transpose shifted inputs of a number of batches\n55\t(“narrow”, eg. MobileNet XY batching).\n56\t\n57\t![CoralNPU MAC](images/coralnpu_aconv.png)\n58\t\n59\tThe outer-product construction is a vertical arrangement of multiple VDOT\n60\topcodes which utilize 4x 8bit multiplies reduced into 32 bit accumulators and\n61\tperforming 256 MACs per cycle.\n62\t\n63\t### Stripmining\n64\t\n65\tStrip mining is defined as folding array-based parallelism to fit the available\n66\thardware parallelism. To reduce frontend instruction dispatch pressure becoming\n67\ta bottleneck, and to natively support instruction level tiling patterns through\n68\tthe SIMD registers, the instruction encoding shall explicitly include a\n69\tstripmine mechanism that converts a single frontend dispatch event to the\n70\tcommand queue into four serialized issue events into the SIMD units. For\n71\tinstance a “vadd v0” in Dispatch will produce “vadd v0 : vadd v1 : vadd v2 :\n72\tvadd v3” at Issue. These will be processed as four discrete events.\n73\t\n74\t## Cache\n75\t\n76\tCaches exists as a single layer between the core and the first level of shared\n77\tSRAM. The L1 cache and scalar core frontend are an overhead to the rest of the\n78\tbackend compute pipeline and ideally are as small as possible.\n79\t\n80\tThe L1Icache is 8KB (256b blocks * 256 slots) with 4-way set associativity.\n81\t\n82\tThe L1Dcache sizing is towards the scalar core requirements to perform loop\n83\tmanagement and address generation. The L1Dcache is 16KB (SIMD256b) with low set\n84\tassociativity of 4-way. The L1Dcache is implemented with a dual bank\n85\tarchitecture where each bank is 8KB (similar to L1Icache). This property allows\n86\tfor a degree of next line prefetch. The L1Dcache also serves as an alignment\n87\tbuffer for the scalar and SIMD instructions to assist development and to\n88\tsimplify software support. In an embedded setting, the L1Dcache provides half of\n89\tthe memory bandwidth to the ML outer-product engine when only a single external\n90\tmemory port is provided. Line and all entry flushing is supported where the core\n91\tstalls until completion to simplify the contract.\n92\t\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. The SystemVerilog can be generated with:\n12\t\n13\t``` bash\n14\tbazel build //hdl/chisel/src/coralnpu:core_mini_axi_cc_library_emit_verilog\n15\t```\n16\t\n17\t### Module interfaces\n18\t\n19\t![CoralNPU AXI](images/coralnpu_axi.svg)\n20\t\n21\tThe interfaces to CoralNPU are defined as follows:\n22\t\n23\t|   Signal Bundle  |                   Description                             |\n24\t| ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |\n25\t|       clk        | The clock of the AXI Bus/CoralNPU core.                     |\n26\t|      reset       | The active-low reset signal for the AXI Bus/CoralNPU core.  |\n27\t|      s_axi       | An AXI4 slave interface that can be used to write TCMs or touch CoralNPU CSRs. |\n28\t|      m_axi       | An AXI4 master interface used by CoralNPU to read/write to memories/CSRs. |\n29\t|       irqn       | Active-low interrupt to the CoralNPU core. Can be triggered by peripherals or other host processor. |\n30\t|       wfi        | Active-high signal from the CoralNPU core, indicating that the core is waiting for an interrupt. While this is active, CoralNPU is clock-gated. |\n31\t|      debug       | Debug interface to monitor CoralNPU instructions execution. This interface is typically only used for simulation. |\n32\t|      halted      | Output interface informing if the Core is running or not. Can be ignored. |\n33\t|      fault       | Output interface to determine if the Core hit a fault. These signals should be connected to a system control CPU interrupt-line or status register for notification when CoralNPU faults or is halted. |\n34\t\n35\t#### AXI master signals\n36\t\n37\tAR / AW channel\n38\t\n39\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n40\t| ------ | --------- |\n41\t| addr   | Address CoralNPU wishes to read/write |\n42\t| prot   | Always 2 (unprivileged, insecure, data) |\n43\t| id     | Always 0 |\n44\t| len    | (Count of beats in the burst) - 1 |\n45\t| size   | Bytes-per-beat (1, 2, or 4) |\n46\t| burst  | Always 1 (INCR) |\n47\t| lock   | Always 0 (normal access) |\n48\t| cache  | Always 0 (Device non-bufferable) |\n49\t| qos    | Always 0 |\n50\t| region | Always 0 |\n51\t\n52\tR channel\n53\t\n54\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n55\t| ------ | --------- |\n56\t| data   | Response data from the slave |\n57\t| id     | Ignored, but should be 0 as CoralNPU only emits txns with an id of 0 |\n58\t| resp   | Response code |\n59\t| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |\n60\t\n61\tW channel\n62\t\n63\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n64\t| ------ | --------- |\n65\t| data   | Data CoralNPU wishes to write |\n66\t| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |\n67\t| strb   | Which bytes in the data are valid |\n68\t\n69\tB channel\n70\t\n71\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n72\t| ------ | --------- |\n73\t| id     | Ignored, but should be 0 as CoralNPU only emits txns with an id of 0 (an RTL assertion exists for this) |\n74\t| resp   | Response code |\n75\t\n76\tNote: the USER signal is not supported on any of the channels.\n77\t\n78\t#### AXI slave signals\n79\t\n80\tAR / AW channel\n81\t\n82\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n83\t| ------ | --------- |\n84\t| addr   | Address the master wishes to read / write to |\n85\t| prot   | Ignored |\n86\t| id     | Transaction ID, should be reflected in the response beats |\n87\t| len    | (Count of beats in the burst) - 1 |\n88\t| size   | Bytes-per-beat (1,2,4,8,16) |\n89\t| burst  | 0, 1, or 2 (FIXED, INCR, WRAP) |\n90\t| lock   | Ignored |\n91\t| cache  | Ignored |\n92\t| qos    | Ignored |\n93\t| region | Ignored |\n94\t\n95\tR channel\n96\t\n97\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n98\t| ------ | --------- |\n99\t| data   | Response data from CoralNPU |\n100\t| id     | Transaction ID, should match with the id field from AR |\n101\t| resp   | Response code (0/OKAY or 2/SLVERR) |\n102\t| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |\n103\t\n104\tW channel\n105\t\n106\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n107\t| ------ | --------- |\n108\t| data   | Data the master wishes to write to CoralNPU |\n109\t| last   | Whether the beat is the last in the burst |\n110\t| strb   | Which bytes in data are valid |\n111\t\n112\tB channel\n113\t\n114\t| Signal | Behaviour |\n115\t| ------ | --------- |\n116\t| id     | Transaction ID, should match with the id field from AW |\n117\t| resp   | Response code (0/OKAY or 2/SLVERR)\n118\t\n119\tNote: the USER signal is not supported on any of the channels.\n120\t\n121\t#### Debug Signals\n122\t\n123\t| Signal   | Behaviour |\n124\t| -------- | --------- |\n125\t| en       | 4-bit value, indicating which fetch lanes are active |\n126\t| addr     | 32-bit values, containing the PC for each fetch lane |\n127\t| inst     | 32-bit values, containing the instruction for each fetch lane |\n128\t| cycles   | cycle counter |\n129\t| dbus     | Information about internal LSU transactions |\n130\t| -> valid | Whether the transaction is valid |\n131\t| -> bits  | addr: The 32-bit address for the transaction |\n132\t|          | write: If the transaction is a write |\n133\t|          | wdata: 128-bit write data for the transaction |\n134\t| dispatch | Information about instructions which are dispatched for execution |\n135\t| -> fire  | If an instruction was dispatched in the slot, this cycle |\n136\t| -> addr  | The 32-bit address of the instruction |\n137\t| -> inst  | The 32-bit value of the instruction |\n138\t| regfile  | Information about writes to the integer register file |\n139\t| -> writeAddr | Register addresses to which a future write is expected |\n140\t| ->-> valid | If an instruction was dispatched in this externally.\n168\t\n169\t## Booting CoralNPU\n170\tA note first -- in these examples, CoralNPU is located in the overall system memory map at 0x70000000.\n171\t\n172\t1. The instruction memory of CoralNPU must be initialized.\n173\t```c\n174\tvolatile uint8_t* coralnpu_itcm = (uint8_t*)0x00000000L;\n175\tfor (int i = 0; i < coralnpu_binary_len; ++i) {\n176\t    coralnpu_itcm[i] = coralnpu_binary[i];\n177\t}\n178\t```\n179\t\n180\tIf something like a DMA engine is present in your system, that is probably a better option for initializing the ITCM.\n181\t\n182\t2. The design\n5\tof CoralNPU starts with domain and matrix capabilities; vector and scalar\n6\tcapabilities are then added for a fused design.\n7\t\n8\t## Block Diagram\n9\t\n10\t![CoralNPU block diagram](images/coralnpu_block.png)\n11\t\n12\t## Scalar Core\n13\t\n14\tA simple RISC-V scalar frontend drives the command queues of the ML+SIMD\n15\tbackend.\n16\t\n17\tCoralNPU utilizes a custom RISC-V frontend (rv32im) that runs the minimal set of\n18\tinstructions to support an executor run-to-completion model (eg. no OS, no\n19\tinterrupts), with all control tasks onloaded to the SMC . The C extension\n20\tencoding is reclaimed (as per the risc-v specification) to provide the necessary\n21\tencoding space for the SIMD registers (6b indices), and to allow flexible type\n22\tencodings and instruction compression (stripmining) for the SIMD instruction\n23\tset. The scalar core is an in order machine with no speculation.\n24\t\n25\tThe branch policy in the fetch stage is backwards branches are taken and forward\n26\tbranches are not-taken, incurring a penalty cycle if the execute result does not\n27\tmatch the decision in the fetch unit.\n28\t\n29\tRegisters        | Names         | Width\n30\t---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------\n31\tScalar (31)      | zero, x1..x31 | 32 bits\n32\tControl & Status | CSRx          | Various\n33\t\n34\t## Vector Core\n35\t\n36\tWe use SIMD and vector interchangeably, referring to a simple and practical SIMD\n37\tinstruction definition devoid of variable length behaviors. The scalar frontend\n38\tis decoupled from the backend by a FIFO structure that buffers vector\n39\tinstructions, posting only to the relevant command queues when dependencies are\n40\tresolved in the vector regfile. The vector core supports data widths of 8, 16, and 32 bits.\n41\t\n42\tRegisters        | Names         | Width\n43\t---------------- | ------------- | -----------------------\n44\tVector (64)      | v0..v63       | 256 bits (eg. int32 x8)\n45\tAccumulator      | acc<8><8>     | 8x8x 32 bits\n46\t\n47\t\n48\t### MAC\n49\t\n50\tThe central component of the design is a quantized outer product\n51\tmultiply-accumulate engine. An outer-product engine provides two-dimensional\n52\tbroadcast structures to maximize the amount of deliverable compute with respect\n53\tto memory accesses. On one axis is a parallel broadcast (“wide”, convolution\n54\tweights), and the other axis the transpose shifted inputs of a number of batches\n55\t(“narrow”, eg. MobileNet XY batching).\n56\t\n57\t![CoralNPU MAC](images/coralnpu_aconv.png)\n58\t\n59\tThe outer-product construction is a vertical arrangement of multiple VDOT\n60\topcodes which utilize 4x 8bit multiplies reduced into 32 bit accumulators and\n61\tperforming 256 MACs per cycle.\n62\t\n63\t### Stripmining\n64\t\n65\tStrip mining is defined as folding array-based parallelism to fit the available\n66\thardware parallelism. To reduce frontend instruction dispatch pressure becoming\n67\ta bottleneck, and to natively support instruction level tiling patterns through\n68\tthe SIMD registers, the instruction encoding shall explicitly include a\n69\tstripmine mechanism that converts a single frontend dispatch event to the\n70\tcommand queue into four serialized issue events into the SIMD units. For\n71\tinstance a “vadd v0” in Dispatch will produce “vadd v0 : vadd v1 : vadd v2 :\n72\tvadd v3” at Issue. These will be processed as four discrete events.\n73\t\n74\t## Cache\n75\t\n76\tCaches exists as a single layer between the core and the first level of shared\n77\tSRAM. The L1 cache and scalar core frontend are an overhead to the rest of the\n78\tbackend compute pipeline and ideally are as small as possible.\n79\t\n80\tThe L1Icache is 8KB (256b blocks * 256 slots) with 4-way set associativity.\n81\t\n82\tThe L1Dcache sizing is towards the scalar core requirements to perform loop\n83\tmanagement and address generation. The L1Dcache is 16KB (SIMD256b) with low set\n84\tassociativity of 4-way. The L1Dcache is implemented with a dual bank\n85\tarchitecture where each bank is 8KB (similar to L1Icache). This property allows\n86\tfor a degree of next line prefetch. The L1Dcache also serves as an alignment\n87\tbuffer for the scalar and SIMD instructions to assist development and to\n88\tsimplify software support. In an embedded setting, the L1Dcache provides half of\n89\tthe memory bandwidth to the ML outer-product engine when only a single external\n90\tmemory port is provided. Line and all entry flushing is supported where the core\n91\tstalls until completion to simplify the contract.\n92\t\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. The instruction stages are:\n9\t\n10\t* **Instruction fetch:** Instructions are fetched from memory into an\n11\tinstruction buffer.\n12\t* **Decode/Dispatch:** The first 4 instructions in the instruction buffer are\n13\tdecoded. Interlock and scoreboard logic determine which of the instructions can\n14\tbe dispatched this cycle. Instructions are forwarded to their respective\n15\texecution units.\n16\t* **Execute/Writeback:** Execution units with dispatched instructions read\n17\toperands from the register file and perform computation. Results can also be\n18\twritten back to the register file in the same cycle.\n19\t\n20\tSome execution units can take multiple cycles to execute. Instruction latencies\n21\tcan be found in the table below:\n22\t\n23\t| Instruction Type | Latency (cycles) | Description            |\n24\t| ---------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |\n25\t| Alu              | 1                | Add, sub, xor, ...     |\n26\t| Csr              | 1                | CSR instructions       |\n27\t| Bru              | 1                | bge, jal, ebreak, ...  |\n28\t| Mlu              | 2                | mul, mulh, ...         |\n29\t| Dvu              | Variable         | div, rem, ...          |\n30\t| Lsu              | 2+               | lw, sw, ...            |\n31\t\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. Functionally,\n6\tit's purpose is to translate memory instructions into transactions on the\n7\tappropriate subsystem.\n8\t\n9\t## Slots\n10\t\n11\tThe CoralNPU LSU uses a concept called _slots_ to handle memory transactions. A\n12\tslot is a data structure which manages the state of a single dispatched LSU\n13\toperation and determines what memory transaction should be performed. At its\n14\tcore, there exists a table in each slot which tracks which part of the memory\n15\toperation has been completed.\n16\t\n17\tFor example, below is the slot table for a word-store into address 0xDEADBEEF:\n18\t\n19\t| Index | Active |   Address  | Data |\n20\t| ----- | ------ | ---------- | ---- |\n21\t|   0   |    1   | 0xDEADBEEF | 0x01 |\n22\t|   1   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF0 | 0x23 |\n23\t|   2   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF1 | 0x45 |\n24\t|   3   |    1   | 0xDEADBEF2 | 0x67 |\n25\t|   4   |    0   | 0xDEADBEF3 | 0x00 |\n26\t...\n27\t|   n   |    0   | 0xDEADBEF3 | 0x00 |\n28\t\n29\tMemory transactions over TCM or AXI busses will read/write data in the slot\n30\ttable and flip the active bits to 0 as they are made.\n31\t\n32\tThe typical lifetime of a slot is as follows:\n33\t\n34\t1) **Idle**: An idle slot will dequeue a LsuOperation from the command queue.\n35\tScalar operations will move directly into **Transfer Memory** while vector\n36\toperations will go to the **Vector Update** state.\n37\t2) **Vector Update**: For vector operations masks, addresses (for indexed ops)\n38\tand data (for store ops) need to be received from the RvvCore. This stage is\n39\tbypassed for scalar operations.\n40\t3) **Transfer Memory**: While there are still active entries in the slot table,\n41\tthe active entry with the lowest \"index\" will be selected for a memory\n42\ttransaction. A scatter/gather unit will then select all other active entries\n43\t(although not necessarily contiguous) that will be bundled with the transaction.\n44\tThe appropriate memory bus (ibus, dbus, ebus) will then be selected and a memory\n45\ttransaction will be conducted. When there are no active entries, the slot moves\n46\tinto the next state (**Writeback**).\n47\t4) **Writeback**: Once all memory transactions are completed, the result must\n48\tbe written back to register files. Additionally, vector stores are\n49\t\"acknowledged\" back to the RvvCore. Scalar and floating point scores bypass this\n50\tstage. Once writeback is completed, the slot moves back into the\n51\t**Vector Update** state for LMUL > 1, or the **Idle** state.\n52\t\n53\tCoralNPU currently uses one \"slot\" in the LSU. In the future, multiple slots maybe\n54\tadded to allow multiple operations to partake in the same transaction.\n55\t\n56\t## Interfaces\n57\t\n58\t### LSU Command Interface\n59\t\n60\tThe LSU has a command interface coming from the dispatch unit and register file.\n61\t\n62\t| Signal Name   | Type          | Description                                                   |\n63\t| ------------- | ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |\n64\t| req.valid     | Bool          | If the LSU command is valid.                                  |\n65\t| req.op        |               | The LSU operation to execute.                                 |\n66\t| req.addr      | UInt(5)       | The RegFile address to write the result to for loads.         |\n67\t| req.pc        | UInt(32)      | The PC of the LSU instruction. MEMORY ARCHITECTURE\n\n#### ITCM (Instruction Tightly-Coupled Memory)\n- **Size:** 8 KB\n- **Address Range:** `0x0000 - 0x1FFF`\n- **Alignment:** 4 bytes\n- **Access:** Scalar-only, from fetch unit\n\n#### DTCM (Data Tightly-Coupled Memory)\n- **Size:** 32 KB\n- **Address Range:** `0x10000 - 0x17FFF`\n- **Alignment:** 1 byte\n- **Access:** Scalar core, SIMD operations, stores\n\n#### External Memory (CSR-Mapped)\n- **CSR Address Range:** `0x30000 - TBD`\n- **Alignment:** 4 bytes\n\n#### Data Width Configurations\nFrom `/app/tests/verilator_sim/coralnpu/coralnpu_cfg.h`:\n- **SIMD Width:** 128, 256, or 512 bits (compile-time configurable)\n- **LSU Data Bus (dbus):** 128 bits minimum (depends on SIMD config)\n- **Fetch Data Bus (ibus):** 256 bits for instruction fetch\n\n---\n\n### 4. AXI INTERFACE SPECIFICATION\n\n#### AXI Master (CoralNPU reads/writes external memory)\n\n**Address/Write Channels (AR/AW):**\n| Signal | Value | Notes |\n|--------|-------|-------|\n| `addr` | Variable | 32-bit address |\n| `prot` | Always 2 | Unprivileged, insecure, data |\n| `id` | Always 0 | No multiple outstanding transactions |\n| `len` | (Count-1) | Burst length |\n| `size` | 1, 2, or 4 | Bytes per beat (8, 16, or 32-bit) |\n| `burst` | Always 1 | INCR mode |\n| `lock` | Always 0 | Normal access |\n| `cache` | Always 0 | Device non-bufferable |\n| `qos` | Always 0 | No QoS |\n\n**Read Data Channel (R):**\n| Signal | Behavior |\n|--------|----------|\n| `data` | Response data |\n| `id` | Always 0 |\n| `resp` | 0=OKAY, 2=SLVERR |\n| `last` | End-of-burst marker |\n\n**Write Data & Response (W/B):**\n| Signal | Behavior |\n|--------|----------|\n| `data` | Write payload |\n| `strb` | Byte enable mask |\n| `last` | End-of-burst marker |\n| `resp` | 0=OKAY, 2=SLVERR |\n\n#### AXI Slave (External master accesses TCMs/CSRs)\n\nSupports all AXI3/4 standard signals:\n- **Address sizes:** 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 bytes per beat\n- **Burst modes:** FIXED, INCR, WRAP\n- **Transaction IDs:** Preserved in responses\n- **Responses:** OKAY or SLVERR\n\n---\n\n### 5. CSR (CONTROL & STATUS REGISTERS) MAP\n\n#### External CSRs (accessed via AXI Slave)\n\n**Boot & Control:**\n| Address | Name | Bits | Description |\n|---------|------|------|-------------|\n| `0x30000` | `RESET_CONTROL` | [1:0] | RESET, CLOCK_GATE |\n| `0x30004` | `PC_START` | [31:0] | Program counter initialization |\n| `0x30008` | `STATUS` | [1:0] | HALTED, FAULT flags |\n\n**Debug Module CSRs (at `0x30800`+):**\n| Address | Name | Purpose |\n|---------|------|---------|\n| `0x30800` | `req_addr` | Debug module register address |\n| `0x30804` | `req_data` | Write data for debug operations |\n| `0x30808` | `req_op` | Operation: NOP(0), READ(1), WRITE(2) |\n| `0x3080C` | `rsp_data` | Read response data |\n| `0x30810` | `rsp_op` | Response status: SUCCESS(0), FAILED(2), BUSY(3) |\n| `0x30814` | `status` | Bit 0: ready, Bit 1: response valid |\n\n#### Internal Debug Module Registers\n\nAccessed via `req_addr`/`req_op` CSRs:\n- `0x04` - `data0` - Abstract command data\n- `0x10` - `dmcontrol` - Control (haltreq, resumereq, ndmreset, dmactive)\n- `0x11` - `dmstatus` - Status (anyrunning, anyhalted, version)\n- `0x16` - `abstractcs` - Abstract command status (busy, cmderr)\n- `0x17` - `command` - Abstract command encoding\n\n**Register Access via Debug Module:**\n- CSRs: `0x0000-0x0FFF`\n- Scalar GPRs (x0-x31): `0x1000-0x101F`\n- Float GPRs (f0-f31): `0x1020-0x103F`\n\n---\n\n### 6. PROCESSOR PIPELINE\n\n**3-Stage In-Order Pipeline:**\n1. **Fetch** → Instruction buffer (4-way dispatch capable)\n2. **Decode/Dispatch** → Up to 4 instructions/cycle with interlock logic\n3. **Execute/Writeback** → Multiple execution units, variable latency\n\n**Instruction Latencies:**\n| Type | Cycles | Examples |\n|------|--------|----------|\n| ALU | 1 | Add, sub, xor, etc. |\n| CSR | 1 | CSR read/write |\n| BRU | 1 | Branch resolution |\n| MLU | 2 | mul, mulh, mulhsu, mulhu |\n| DVU | Variable | div, rem, divu, remu |\n| LSU | 2+ | Load/store with data wait |\n\n**Scalar Registers:** 31 registers (x1-x31, x0=zero)  \n**Vector Registers:** 64 registers (v0-v63), 256 bits each (configurable)\n\n---\n\n### 7. LOAD/STORE UNIT (LSU)\n\n**Slot-Based Architecture:** Single slot manages memory operations with state table tracking sub-word transactions.\n\n**Three Internal Buses:**\n1. **IBUS** (Instruction bus) - Read-only, 256-bit, from ITCM\n2. **DBUS** (Data bus) - Read/write, 128-bit, from DTCM\n3. **EBUS** (External bus) - Read/write, 128-bit, via AXI to external memory\n\n**DBUS/EBUS Interface Signals:**\n| Signal | Type | Width | Meaning |\n|--------|------|-------|---------|\n| `valid` | Bool | 1 | Transaction valid |\n| `addr` | UInt | 32 | Memory address |\n| `size` | UInt | 5 | Transaction size in bytes |\n| `pc` | UInt | 32 | Instruction PC (for fault reporting) |\n| `wdata` | UInt | 128 | Write data |\n| `wmask` | UInt | 16 | Byte write mask |\n| `rdata` | UInt | 128 | Read data (input, +1 cycle latency) |\n| `fault.valid` | Bool | 1 | Fault occurred |\n| `fault.write` | Bool | 1 | Was a write operation |\n| `fault.addr` | UInt | 32 | Fault address |\n| `fault.epc` | UInt | 32 | Instruction PC when fault triggered |\n\n---\n\n### 8. DEBUG INTERFACE\n\n#### Instruction Debug Output\n\nFrom `core_mini_axi_tb.h`, the testbench monitors:\n- **4 fetch lanes** with per-cycle: enable, PC, instruction\n- **Dispatch info** per lane: fire, address, instruction\n- **Register file writes**: Address prediction + actual writes (6 ports)\n- **Floating-point writes**: Address prediction + actual writes (2 ports)\n- **RVV writes** (if enabled): Vector register updates with data/index per lane\n\n#### Debug CSR Access Protocol\n\n1. Poll `status` at `0x30814` for bit 0 (ready)\n2. Write address to `req_addr` at `0x30800`\n3. Write operation code to `req_op` at `0x30808`\n4. For writes: pre-load `req_data` at `0x30804`\n5. Poll `status` for bit 1 (response valid)\n6. Read `rsp_op` at `0x30810` (SUCCESS=0, FAILED=2, BUSY=3)\n7. For reads: read `rsp_data` at `0x3080C`\n\n---\n\n### 9. RTL modules register SRAMs with backdoor at simulation startup\n2. Each SRAM has a global address range and width\n3. Backdoor loader maintains a map of `addr -> BackdoorSram*`\n4. DEBUG INTERFACE\n\n#### Instruction Debug Output\n\nFrom `core_mini_axi_tb.h`, the testbench monitors:\n- **4 fetch lanes** with per-cycle: enable, PC, instruction\n- **Dispatch info** per lane: fire, address, instruction\n- **Register file writes**: Address prediction + actual writes (6 ports)\n- **Floating-point writes**: Address prediction + actual writes (2 ports)\n- **RVV writes** (if enabled): Vector register updates with data/index per lane\n\n#### Debug CSR Access Protocol\n\n1. Poll `status` at `0x30814` for bit 0 (ready)\n2. Write address to `req_addr` at `0x30800`\n3. Write operation code to `req_op` at `0x30808`\n4. For writes: pre-load `req_data` at `0x30804`\n5. Poll `status` for bit 1 (response valid)\n6. Read `rsp_op` at `0x30810` (SUCCESS=0, FAILED=2, BUSY=3)\n7. For reads: read `rsp_data` at `0x3080C`\n\n---\n\n### 9. SRAM BACKDOOR MECHANISM\n\n**Purpose:** Fast, direct SRAM initialization for simulation without going through AXI transactions.\n\n**Implementation:** (`sram_backdoor.cc/h`)\n\n**C++ Interface:**\n```cpp\nbool SramBackdoorLoad(uint64_t global_addr, const uint8_t* data, size_t len)\n```\n\n**Python Interface:** (`backdoor.py`)\n```python\ndef backdoor_load(addr, data):\n    \"\"\"Loads data into simulator SRAM via DPI C function.\"\"\"\n```\n\n**Mechanism:**\n1. RTL modules register SRAMs with backdoor at simulation startup\n2. Each SRAM has a global address range and width\n3. Backdoor loader maintains a map of `addr -> BackdoorSram*`\n4. When `backdoor_load()` called, it finds overlapping SRAMs and directly memcpy data\n5. ELF parsing support via `sram_load_elf()` for batch loading\n\n**Key Features:**\n- Supports late binding (data loaded before SRAMs registered)\n- Automatic range matching across multiple SRAMs\n- Direct memory access (bypasses normal simulation transaction delays)\n- SRAM handles register calls via DPI: `sram_init()`, `sram_read()`, `sram_write()`, `sram_cleanup()`\n\n---\n\n### 10. TEST INFRASTRUCTURE\n\n#### Verilator-Based Simulation\n\n**Testbench:** `CoreMiniAxi_tb` (SystemC wrapper)\n- Binds TLM/AXI bridges for master/slave traffic\n- Connects debug signals for instruction tracing\n- Supports ELF file loading (sync or async)\n- Clock gating and reset control\n- Backdoor loading and status polling\n\n#### Cocotb-Based Tests\n\n**Harness:** `CoreMiniAxiInterface` (Python)\n- Drives AXI signals: read/write address, data, response\n- Manages external memory model (`0x20000000` onwards)\n- TCM size configuration (via binary rule parameters)\n- CSR access helper functions\n- Clock generation\n\n#### Example TCM Sizes\n\nDefault from integration guide:\n- ITCM: 8 KB at `0x0000`\n- DTCM: 32 KB at `0x10000`\n- Customizable via build rules\n\n---\n\n### 11. Determine sign (for signed conversion, check the MSB).\n    *   2. Compute the absolute value.\n    *   3. Count leading zeros to find the position of the implicit leading 1.\n    *   4.
